newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro Disney loss widens, charges rise.
newsitem.headline: Euro Disney loss widens, charges rise.

text.p: Euro Disney said Tuesday its losses widened in the first half of 1996-97 as rising debt expenses swallowed up income generated by the Disneyland Paris theme park.

Euro Disney reported a net loss of 210 million francs ($36 million) for the six months to March 31, its winter season, compared with a loss of 169 million francs ($29 million) for the first half of 1995/96.

The deterioration in its results, the first year-on-year downturn after more than two years of improvement, was due to a 68-million-franc ($12 million) jump in charges to 356 million francs ($61 million).

The surge in lease and financial expenses had been expected as Euro Disney took on payments that had been temporarily waived by a 1994 debt restructuring accord to keep the fledgling company from collapsing under a huge debt burden.

Excluding the charges, first-half income more than doubled to 120 million francs ($12 million) from 58 million ($10 million) on sales of 2.17 billion francs ($372 million), helped by a 12.5 percent rise in attendance, higher hotel occupancy rates and increased spending per visitor.
The commercial appeal of Euro Disney, 39 percent owned by The Walt Disney Co., is no longer in doubt. It celebrated its fifth anniversary last month as Europe's top tourist attraction.

"The success of Disneyland Paris is growing, as is our ability to manage the seasonal fluctuations in the business. However, growth in the high season remains vital to counter the sharp increases in financial charges," Chairman Gilles Pelisson said in the earnings statement.
The company traditionally loses money in the winter season but more than compensates during the April-September high season and has reported full-year profits for the past two years.

The first-half results were in line with stock market expectations. But the stock price fell 1 percent to 9.80 francs ($1.68) as the results reminded investors that gains in operating profit would go to pay back the banks and to Disney.
